Step 1 · Contrast

A Poem That Tells a Story

A sonnet thinks. A ballad tells a story. Today: a wild horse chase in the Australian mountains.

Did you know? Banjo Paterson published The Man from Snowy River in 1890, in a Sydney magazine called The Bulletin. Australians loved it, and many learnt it by heart. Paterson’s face is on the Australian $10 note, and you can find a line from this poem printed on it in tiny letters.

Note: A ballad is a poem that tells a story. The first ballads were songs, passed on by people singing them aloud. A bush ballad is the Australian kind: stories about horses, cattle, droving, and hard life in “the bush”, the wild country away from the cities.
You know this one

Sonnet

14 lines, one block of thought.

One feeling or argument, with a turn (“But…”).

Examples: Sonnet 43 (Browning), Sonnet 18 (Shakespeare)

New today

Ballad

Many stanzas (groups of lines), as long as the story needs.

A story: characters, action, a beginning, a middle and an end.

Example: The Man from Snowy River, Banjo Paterson

Visit Snowy River

Where is Snowy River country?

The poem happens in the Snowy Mountains in south-east Australia, between Sydney and Melbourne. The Snowy River starts high up near Mount Kosciuszko, Australia’s highest mountain, and runs down through New South Wales into Victoria. Can you find the Snowy River and the town of Jindabyne (say it JIN-da-bine, rhymes with “fine”) on the map?

Mount Kosciuszko: 36.456° S, 148.264° E (2,228 metres high). Open in Google Maps: Mount Kosciuszko · the Snowy River (open in a new tab).

        Your task

        A first taste

        Read the first stanza aloud, quite fast, then answer: What has happened? Who has come to the station? Can you hear a rhythm like galloping hooves?

        Bush ballad

        The Man from Snowy River (Banjo Paterson): stanza 1

        There was movement at the station, for the word had passed around
          That the colt from old Regret had got away,
        And had joined the wild bush horses — he was worth a thousand pound,
          So all the cracks had gathered to the fray.
        All the tried and noted riders from the stations near and far
          Had mustered at the homestead overnight,
        For the bushmen love hard riding where the wild bush horses are,
          And the stock-horse snuffs the battle with delight.

        station = a big Australian farm  •  colt = a young male horse  •  Regret = the colt’s mother, a famous horse  •  the cracks = the best riders  •  the fray = the fight, the action  •  mustered = gathered together

        Step 2 · The Story

        How a Ballad Is Built

        A sonnet is one room. A ballad is a road: each stanza moves the story one step on.

        The shape of one stanza

        Eight lines: long, short, long, short

        Every stanza in this poem has the same shape. The long lines push the action forward. The short lines land each idea.

        Along
        Bshort
        Along
        Bshort
        Clong
        Dshort
        Clong
        Dshort

        Rhyme: ABABCDCD  Then the next stanza starts with new rhymes.

        The story mountain

        A story climbs slowly to one big moment (the climax), then comes down quickly to the ending. In this poem the big moment really is on a mountain.

        1Stanzas 1–2

        The problem

        A valuable colt has run off. The best riders gather.

        2Stanzas 3–5

        The hero

        A young rider on a small pony. The old man says no. Clancy says yes.

        3Stanzas 6–8

        The chase

        The wild horses escape up the mountain.

        4Stanzas 9–10

        The climax

        He rides straight down the terrible slope, alone.

        5Stanzas 11–13

        The ending

        He brings the horses back. People still tell the story.

        Meet the riders

        Who’s who

        Harrison, “the old man”

        An old, rich rider with white hair. He is in charge of the chase. He thinks the boy is too small.

        Clancy of the Overflow

        The best horseman there. He speaks up for the boy. (Paterson wrote a whole poem about Clancy too.)

        The man from Snowy River

        A stripling (a thin young man, not fully grown) from the mountains, on a small, thin pony. Everyone doubts him. Notice: we never learn his name.

        The colt from old Regret

        A young horse worth “a thousand pound”, a huge amount of money. He has run off with the wild horses.

        Listen first

        Hear it read aloud

        Ballads were made to be heard. Listen once with your eyes closed and feel the gallop. Then listen again and follow the text below.

        Say it right

        How do you say Kosciuszko?

        The poem’s mountain is Mount Kosciuszko, the highest mountain in Australia. Paterson spells it the old way, Kosciusko. The name is Polish, and Australians say it a little differently. The video starts at 0:37, where you hear the Australian way to say it.

        Line by line: what does it mean?

        Read each line aloud. Try to say what it means in your own words. Then tap the line to check. Some notes cover two or more lines, because one sentence runs across them.

        Hidden echo

        Paterson borrows from the Bible

        Look at the last line of stanza 1: “And the stock-horse snuffs the battle with delight.” In the Bible (the Book of Job), God describes a brave war horse that “smelleth the battle afar off”. Paterson’s stock-horse is like that war horse: it can smell the excitement coming, and it loves it.

        Browning did something similar in Sonnet 43. Poets often borrow a famous old line and give it a new home.

        Your task

        Why no name?

        We learn the names of Harrison and Clancy, and even the colt’s mother. But the hero is only ever “the man from Snowy River”. Why do you think Paterson never tells us his name? What does the title tell us is most important about him?

        Step 3 · Rhythm & Rhyme

        The Gallop

        The sonnets went da-DUM, five times, like a calm heartbeat. The long lines of this ballad are faster. They go DUM-da, again and again, like a horse at full gallop.

        DUM-da DUM-da DUM-da DUM-da DUM-da DUM-da DUM-da DUM

        A long line, from stanza 10

        THROUGH the STRIN-gy BARKS and SAP-lings, ON the ROUGH and BRO-ken GROUND

        15 syllables. 8 strong beats. Say it fast and it sounds like hooves.

        The short lines are an old friend. Most short lines in this poem are iambic pentameter, the same da-DUM beat as the sonnets: so ALL the CRACKS had GATH-ered TO the FRAY. So each stanza swaps between a gallop (long line) and a steady trot (short line).

        Activity 3

        Write a long line and a short line

        Write the start of a stanza about anything that moves fast: a storm, a race, a dog chasing a ball. Aim for about 15 syllables in the long line and about 10 in the short line. They don’t need to rhyme yet.

        Example: Down the beach the dog went racing when I threw the ball too far, / and sand flew up behind him like a wave.

        Step 4 · Idea Spark

        Find Your Story

        Start with a story, not with rhymes. The best ballad stories have someone nobody believed in.

        An underdog story. Here is how Paterson builds his:
        • The problem: a valuable horse is lost, and it is a hard job.
        • The hero, and the doubters: a small rider on a small pony. “That horse will never do.”
        • The big moment: the others stop. He goes down the mountain anyway.
        • The ending: he wins, and people tell his story for years.
        The doubters make the ending feel bigger. If nobody had doubted him, it would just be a ride.

        Brainstorm

        Write fast. Single words are fine. Nothing has to rhyme yet. Your story can be true or made up: a sports match, a rescue, a race, a day someone surprised everyone.

        Paterson’s action verbs, to borrow: raced, swung, charged, flew, followed, cleared, plied, halted, wheeled, thundered.

        Plan your ballad

        Poet’s tip: know your big moment first. Everything before it is the climb. Everything after it is the way home.

        Step 5 · Draft Together

        Draft Live

        Write your first stanza: four lines, long, short, long, short. Old ballads often used four-line stanzas. Paterson doubled them to eight.
